headline: The timing fault you picked is fixed. Our speed measurements could report an interrupt costing more than the whole frame that contained it — now each frame is charged what actually ran in it.
matters: Anyone reading our per-frame speed figures was at risk of chasing a spike that had been moved there from the frame before. The engine team had three measurement tools held back over this; they can now judge whether to move them. The fix also turned up that a feature they asked us to build would not have given them what they wanted, so I have flagged it rather than building it.
detail: Q-PROF-STRADDLE settled as a DEFECT (fork A), merged 51143a5 from branch prof-straddle. Root cause: the per-frame ring cut hintCycles/vintCycles from pending_buckets[level].cycles, an INCLUSIVE figure, and inclusive time only reaches a parent when the callee pops. Because the acknowledge arms a routine frame for the handler's own entry address, a bucket's ENTIRE cost is child time and none reaches the bucket before the RTE — so a straddling handler gave frame N the exception entry alone and frame N+1 the whole span. Fix charges the split on the self side via Frame::enclosing_bucket (stack index of innermost bucket, O(1) at push) + Profiler::pending_bucket_retired, accumulated only while the ring is armed. VERIFIED FIRSTHAND AT THIS SEAT, not accepted on report: full workspace suite 1809 passed / 0 failed / 6 ignored exit 0; red-first REPRODUCED by checking out 68461a7 into a scratch worktree and running it — 37 passed / 2 failed with failure output showing vint_cycles 40 against frame cycles 30, and 80 against 50, i.e. an interrupt costing more than its containing frame, which is what makes it arithmetic rather than taste; merged tree re-verified 41/0. Currency unmoved — golden_frames 7/0, scanline goldens, conformance_roms 3/0 in 41.7s of real work (checked for the silent-skip failure this repo has booked; vendor symlink present, no SKIP markers), schema_conformance 21/0 so no wire drift. RETRACTIONS the agent made against our own records, both correct: the mechanism doc's own SS2 'correction' was wrong (it reasoned from the generic parent/child rule and never asked what a bucket's children ARE), so the original SS3.3(a) finding was right; and SS3/SS6 rested on 'a bucket's cyclesSelf is lag-free', which is true and useless — corroborated by a PRE-EXISTING test, a_nested_hint_inside_a_vint_charges_the_inner_bucket_alone, pinning hint.self_cycles at one STEP_CYCLES against hint.cycles of three. That undercuts PROF-RING-SELF as specified; recommendation to refuse recorded, owner's call, not built. Also merged: new overseer bar that agents must not edit lane-status.json, after this one wrote an enum the suite contract does not define.

headline: Told aeon not to build the profiler field they asked for — and proved why on their own game rather than arguing it.
matters: They wanted a per-frame number showing what each interrupt cost. The field as they specified it would have been a constant: measured on their own ROM, it comes out to exactly 44 for both kinds of interrupt, even though one genuinely costs 19 times more than the other. It would have printed the same value during a slowdown as without one — a field that looks like the answer and is not. The number they actually want is one they already read, and it now accounts for every last cycle exactly. Building it would have cost real time and left them measuring nothing; the honest refusal is the more useful delivery.

Also the first on-machine validation of the straddle fix (4111c88 / merge 51143a5), which §7 of the mechanism doc settled on synthetic streams only. headline: We can't honestly say which game object a clicked sprite is — and now we know exactly why, and what would fix it.
matters: You wanted to click something in the game window and be told what it is. The emulator can see which hardware sprite you clicked, and it can read the game's object list, but nothing in the running machine connects the two — the engine draws the sprites and keeps no record of which object drew which. Every shortcut for guessing it fails on rings, which are the thing you are most likely to click and which are not objects at all, so a guess would confidently name the wrong thing with nothing to warn you. So the window will say plainly that it cannot tell you, rather than inventing an answer. The fix is small and it lives in the engine, not here: one debug-only list, 160 bytes, that writes down which object drew each sprite as it draws it. That ask is now with the engine lane, priced, with the line numbers checked against their tree. If they take it, clicking an object works properly and can even tell when the picture has moved on since you clicked.

headline: Tools can now write into video memory — through the path that keeps the sprite table honest, not the shortcut that would have lied.
matters: The editor and the engine lane both want to push artwork straight into the running machine to see it immediately, without a rebuild. There was already a shortcut in the code that looked like the obvious way to do it, and using it would have quietly broken things: the emulator keeps a small cached copy of where each sprite is, and the shortcut skips updating it, so the machine would have drawn a picture that its own memory did not describe. The new path keeps that copy in step. Three places where the written-down rules are silent - whether this should be refused while the game is running, what addresses it may touch, how much it may write at once - were implemented as the rules actually read and filed as questions upstream, rather than being quietly decided here. That order matters: adding a refusal later is easy, removing one people have built on is not.

headline: When the debugger stops the game, it sometimes stops a little late — and we found someone had already measured how often.
matters: Stopping the game at an exact instruction is the core of debugging, and until now nothing told you whether the stop landed where you asked or slightly past it. We proposed that every emulator must declare its own precision up front. While checking whether the problem was still real, an agent went looking in the old emulator's own documentation and found it had been measured years back and written down: most stops are exact, but one trial in four stopped 98 bytes early. That single fact changed the design from a preference into a requirement - if the imprecision comes and goes, you cannot learn about it by watching, because four good stops tell you nothing about the fifth. So a server has to promise its worst case rather than describe its usual one. The proposal is honest about its own weakness: everyone using this today is on the old emulator that is being retired, so it makes their move across checkable rather than making today better.

headline: Breakpoints work on the new emulator — you can stop the game on an exact instruction and look around.
matters: This is the thing a developer reaches for most and the new emulator did not have it at all. Five commands now work: set a stop point, turn it on or off, list what is armed, clear it, and wait for the game to hit one. It takes the list of missing commands from fifteen down to ten. The care went into one decision that would have been invisible if it had gone wrong: when a client asks to wait for the game to stop, the waiting happens on that client's own connection rather than inside the emulator, because the emulator is what has to keep running to REACH the stop point - a wait done the naive way would have frozen your player window for up to five minutes and then timed out having never moved. Testing also caught the emulator telling two different stories at once: it kept running while every reply said it had stopped, which showed up as 374,011 stops recorded where there should have been one. One honest limitation: a stop point does not fire while the player window is running the game freely on its own. It works everywhere else, including every tool that would use it, and I would rather tell you than let you find out.

headline: Breakpoints now work in your player window — before this, they could not fire at all while you were playing.
matters: Last night's breakpoint work shipped with a limitation I told you about: a stop point would not fire while your game window was running the game freely. I sent an agent to work out how the emulator should honestly SAY that, and the answer came back that there was nothing honest to say. The gap was not partial, it was total: while you were actually playing, a stop point could not fire by any route. Publishing that would have amounted to announcing that the debugger does not work while you debug. So I closed it instead. Your window now stops itself when a stop point is hit, the same way it does when you pause by hand, and it announces the stop to any tool watching. The note that had deferred this priced it as expensive; that was wrong, and the code's own comments said so while the note said otherwise - both pieces it claimed were missing already existed. I proved it works by driving the rebuilt program myself, but that test drove the emulator on its own rather than inside your window; the in-window behaviour is covered by an automated test rather than by me watching a real window, because the only two windows on this machine right now are yours and the editor's, and driving either would disturb your work. headline: I nearly raised a false alarm about our own program being out of date. The alarm was my measuring tool, not the program.
matters: The engine lane was about to rename part of how their tools talk to our emulator, and I checked our side was ready first. It was. But while checking I searched our built program for three pieces of text it should contain, and all three came back missing - which would have meant we were shipping something older than we thought, right as they were about to depend on it. I ran the search five different ways to be sure. All five agreed, and all five were wrong: when the compiler builds the fast version of a program it stores short pieces of text in a form a search cannot see. The engine lane settled it in one command by starting the program and asking it directly, which is the thing I had been avoiding. Two lessons, and the second is the uncomfortable one. First, searching a built program is not a substitute for running it - and it fails in the direction that invents problems. Second, a number I had measured days ago travelled to their notes, came back to me as if it were theirs, and I used it to argue against my own finding. Reading it carefully out of their files did not protect me, because careful reading confirms that a number was copied correctly, not that it was ever right.

headline: A peer found a hole in how we prove the emulator is honest about which build it is, and it was real.
matters: When a tool connects to the emulator, the emulator tells it which exact build of itself is answering - the commit it was built from, and whether that code had uncommitted edits. The editor lane spotted it by reading our tests against each other, which is a thing none of the tests' authors could have done from inside their own. headline: Your click-to-select-and-spawn idea: the hard half is proven working, and the engine lane's job just shrank to nothing for the first stage.
matters: You asked whether we could click things in the running game to select them and click places to spawn them. The engine lane's whole estimate hung on one question: does our click land on an actual game object, or only on a coloured pixel? If the engine had to answer that, their side was a big job. I proved it on a live game instead of guessing: clicking the player told us it was slot 0, 'Player_Main', with its position - and clicking the two rings on screen correctly answered 'that is not an object' rather than confidently naming the wrong one. Clicking a spot also gives its position in the level exactly, checked against where the game itself thinks the player is. All of that uses things the emulator already does, so for the first stage - click to select and inspect - the engine needs no changes at all, and the one thing I had asked them for turned out to be unnecessary and is withdrawn. Two traps found and written into the design so nobody walks into them later: two of the three sprites on screen were rings, so the guard against misreading them matters on the very first click, not in some rare case; and the game's camera lives at a different memory address in the debug build than the shipped one, which would silently place every click in the wrong spot for anyone who wrote the address down instead of looking it up. headline: Click-to-select is built: clicking a spot in the running game now tells you which object drew it, and where that is in the level.
matters: The first half of your click-to-select idea works. Ask the emulator about any dot on screen and it answers three things: which layer you are looking at, where that point sits in the level, and which object slot painted it. The care went into the five different ways the answer can be 'not an object', which sound like pedantry and are not: a ring is drawn differently from a normal object, and on the first real screen this was tried, two of the three things on screen were rings. If the emulator treated a ring like an object it would confidently name the WRONG object rather than admit it did not know - and you would have no way to tell. The same care covers your shipped game versus your debug build: on a shipped build it says 'this build cannot answer that' instead of 'there is nothing there'. Two checks that no automatic rule could catch shipped alongside it, because both are about the emulator telling the truth rather than about the shape of its answer. Also: it looks up where things live in memory every single time rather than remembering, because those addresses MOVE between your debug and shipped builds - and a remembered one gives a wrong answer that looks completely normal. I proved that one by deliberately breaking it: the broken version returned a perfectly plausible position, with no error at all. The spawn half - clicking to place things - is not built and still waits on the engine lane.

headline: The engine lane found a real bug in our emulator, and the right answer turned out to be NOT fixing it.
matters: They reported that clicking a pixel gives the right palette slot but the wrong colour, on any screen where the game changes colours partway down the picture. It is real - I reproduced it on a different test game by a different method, 55 out of 55 sample points wrong. Then I read the rulebook for that command and it says, in as many words, that this command must NOT read the drawn picture, and that this exact disagreement is deliberate and must not be papered over - it names the other command a person should use instead, which is the one the engine lane had already found for themselves. What was actually broken is smaller and real: the answer never tells you which moment its colour belongs to, so two fields quietly disagree and you cannot tell. That is a change to the agreed rules rather than to our code, and it is what I will write next. Two small things did land - a test that pins the behaviour AND explains why the tempting fix is wrong, so the next person does not repeat me, and a note about a rounding convention that was silently making correct pixels look wrong.

headline: The old emulator never checks what it is asked to do - misspell an address and it writes to address zero and says it worked.
matters: The debugging tools every lane in the suite uses still talk to that old server. There is no error for a mistyped parameter anywhere in it: six of its commands quietly fall back to address zero or value zero and reply success. This is the strongest argument yet for finishing the move to the new one, and it is the sentence your README should carry rather than the vaguer 'the surface is legacy' one. Nothing is known to have been bitten by it - this is the exposure, not an incident.
detail: F-LEGACY-SILENT-DEFAULT, docs/2026-08-30-legacy-silent-default.md. oracle-old/linux-port/gui/ControlSocket.cpp:130 getInt(k, d=0) returns d on absent key, unparseable string (catch(...)) and unhandled type; no unknown-key rejection in the file, verified as genuine absence under a positive control (grep -q exit 1, control exit 0). 34 call sites, 8 with no explicit default, 2 of those has()-guarded (:1954,:1959), leaving 6 unguarded and all on memory paths (:348,:702,:726,:782 addr; :615,:739 value). aeon's :894 timeout_ms/30000 confirmed. Protocol bar 15's precedent measured in our own tree. Arrived as aeon's aside about OUR tree in mail (bar 20 shape), verified rather than banked, and their version understated it - they named one site, the defect is the accessor.

headline: Corrected my own finding from this morning: the old emulator ignores 63 parameters, not 34 - and a peer found that by accident.
matters: The headline did not move - six commands still fall back to address zero and report success, and the engine team independently confirmed those line for line. What moved is the scale: I had counted two of the four ways that server reads a parameter, and all four silently substitute a default. I found out because the engine team swept the file more broadly for their own reasons, not because anyone checked my work. Also good news from them: they audited their own tools against it and are clean, 14 calls, no misspellings, no incident.
detail: Family is get(str) :119/18 sites, getInt :130/23, getU32 :152/11, getBool :156/11 = 63, all if(!has(k)) return d. Original doc counted getInt|getU32 only = 34, accurate as counted, understating the 'validates nothing' claim it supported. Protocol bar 19 (enumeration parameter, wrong alphabet) turned on this seat; bar 21 (discriminator fired by accident) - aeon enumerated every get*("key") to build their consumer vocabulary check, not to audit me. Six memory-path sites unchanged and independently re-read by aeon. Consumer side clean per aeon c584df3d: 14 memory-path calls across 3 legacy-seam tools, all correct. Their caveat kept: a clean grep is not a gate on a seam that cannot report a regression.

headline: Closed the count on the old emulator at 64 parameter reads, and found one route that does the OPPOSITE of what the caller asked.
matters: The count is now complete rather than climbing - we swept every way that server can reach a parameter, so nobody has to wonder if there is a 65th. The new one is the sharpest yet: ask it to enable a graphics layer while spelling the value in a way it does not recognise, and it mutes the layer instead, reporting success. It does echo back what it decided, so a careful caller can catch it. Also worth recording that I nearly published a second inversion that was not real - three spots looked unguarded and were guarded two lines up.
detail: Population closed at 64 = 63 accessor sites + ParseButtons :1576 (the only type-checking read; misspelled 'buttons' presses nothing, returns success). Swept 59 const JsonObj& signatures; only raw-json touches are :117/:122/:133/:159 inside the accessors plus :1579-80. JsonObj exposes only p + 4 accessors, so the routes are covered. Type gap: has() :117 true for any present non-null; getBool :156 accepts only true/1/yes from a string, else d. So {'enabled':'on'} passes the explicit has-guard at :1523/:1567/:1925, reads false, *flag=!on mutes. Mitigated by addBool('enabled',on) echo. Near-miss banked: bar 11, read the lines around the cited line. 64th site found by aeon varying enumeration parameter ON PURPOSE - first deliberate bar-19 invocation this lane has seen.

headline: Retracted this morning's finding and replaced it: I named the wrong four commands, and the reason I got it wrong is the same reason twice.
matters: The danger is real and unchanged in size - but it is in different commands than I told you, so anyone acting on the morning version would have hardened the wrong things and left two genuinely open ones alone. The part that survives and is arguably worse: the safety checks those commands do have only catch a MISSING value, never a malformed one. Send a nonsense address as text and every one of them quietly turns it into zero. The engine team found my error, and their own confirmation of it had been hollow - they checked the lines I cited existed rather than that they said what I claimed.
detail: RETRACTED: {:348,:615,:739,:782} are inside if(req.has(...)) and ErrorReply on absence. MISSED BY BOTH: :2110/:2140 read_vram/write_vram getU32('addr',0) unguarded. True set {read_vram.addr, write_vram.addr, z80_read.addr, z80_write.addr}. Root cause: enumerated 'no explicit default' as a proxy for 'unguarded' - orthogonal, giving 4 false positives and excluding the 2 real ones by construction. Third enumeration-parameter failure today; same doc had applied bar 11 correctly to its getBool sites and not to these. Type hazard undiminished at all six: has() passes any present non-null, getInt stoll throws to catch(...)->0, so addr:'0xZZZZ' defeats every guard. 4th correction: getBool string arm returns false not d - material at 5 getBool(k,true) sites (:465,:871,:1366,:1377,:1710). aeon withdrew their corroboration and their consumer 'clean' result (14/3 files -> 131/12 files; live instance: 12 sites send reset{wait:true}, OpReset never reads wait).
